sensation.def: The process by which sense organs detect energy from the world (light, sound, chemicals, pressure) and send it to the brain as neural signals.

transduction.def: The conversion of one form of energy, such as light or sound waves, into neural signals by sensory receptor cells.

absolute-threshold.def: The smallest amount of a stimulus a person can detect half of the time.

jnd.def: The just-noticeable difference (difference threshold): the smallest change in a stimulus a person can detect half of the time.

webers-law.def: The principle that the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, so a bigger stimulus needs a bigger change to be noticed.

signal-detection.def: The theory that whether a faint stimulus is detected depends on both its strength and the person's state, expectations and the costs of a miss or a false alarm.

sensory-adaptation.def: A drop in sensitivity to a stimulus that stays the same, such as no longer smelling a room after a few minutes.

sensory-interaction.def: One sense affecting another, such as smell shaping the flavor of food.

synesthesia.def: A condition in which stimulating one sense also triggers another, such as seeing colors when hearing music or reading numbers.

vision.def: The sense of sight: the eye focuses light on the retina, where rods and cones transduce it into neural signals sent to the occipital lobe.

retina.def: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that contains the rods and cones.

rods.def: Receptors in the retina that work in dim light and detect black, white and gray but not color; most are outside the fovea.

cones.def: Receptors in the retina that detect color and fine detail and need bright light; they are packed in the fovea.

fovea.def: A small pit at the center of the retina, packed with cones, where vision is sharpest.

optic-nerve.def: The bundle of axons that carries visual signals from the retina to the brain.

blind-spot.def: The point where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it has no rods or cones, so light falling there is not detected.

trichromatic.def: The theory that color vision depends on three types of cones, most sensitive to red, green or blue light, whose combined signals code every color.

opponent-process.def: The theory that color is coded by paired, opposing processes (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white), which explains afterimages in the opposite color.

afterimage.def: An image that stays after the stimulus is gone; after staring at a color, its opposite color appears.

color-deficiency.def: Trouble telling some colors apart because one type of cone is missing or works poorly; red-green deficiency is most common and is inherited, mostly in males.

prosopagnosia.def: Face blindness: being unable to recognize familiar faces even though vision is otherwise normal.

blindsight.def: Responding to visual stimuli a person reports not seeing, after damage to the visual cortex.

hearing.def: The sense of sound (audition): sound waves are funneled to the eardrum and middle-ear bones and transduced by hair cells in the cochlea.

cochlea.def: The snail-shaped, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear whose hair cells turn vibrations into neural signals.

place-theory.def: The theory that we hear different pitches because different places along the cochlea vibrate most; it best explains high pitches.

frequency-theory.def: The theory that the rate at which auditory neurons fire matches the frequency of the sound wave; it best explains low pitches.

volley.def: The volley principle: groups of auditory neurons take turns firing so that together they match a sound's frequency, extending frequency theory to middle pitches.

conduction-deafness.def: Hearing loss from damage to the parts that conduct sound to the cochlea: the ear canal, eardrum or middle-ear bones.

sensorineural.def: Hearing loss from damage to the hair cells of the cochlea or to the auditory nerve, often from loud noise or aging; it is usually permanent.

olfaction.def: The sense of smell: receptors high in the nose detect airborne chemicals. Unlike the other senses, its signals do not pass through the thalamus first.

gustation.def: The sense of taste: taste buds detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami and probably fat.

umami.def: The savory taste, detected by receptors for glutamate, found in broth, soy sauce, tomatoes and aged cheese.

oleogustus.def: The proposed basic taste of fat, distinct from its texture.

supertaster.def: A person with many more taste buds than average who tastes some flavors, especially bitter ones, much more intensely.

gate-control.def: The theory that the spinal cord has a neural "gate" that can block pain signals or let them through to the brain; rubbing a hurt spot or distraction can partly close it.

phantom-limb.def: Sensations, including pain, felt in a limb that has been amputated, showing that the brain produces the experience of pain.

vestibular.def: The sense of balance and head movement, from fluid-filled canals and sacs in the inner ear.

kinesthesis.def: The sense of the position and movement of body parts, from receptors in muscles, tendons and joints.
